t: Find Mirror Score of a String — Per-Letter Stacks
o: Scan left to right; at index i, if some unmarked j < i has s[j] = mirror(s[i]) ('a'<->'z', 'b'<->'y', ...), mark both and add i - j; prefer the closest such j. In "aczzx": index 2 ('z') pairs with 0 ('a') for +2, index 4 ('x') pairs with 1 ('c') for +3, total 5. The closest-unmarked requirement is exactly stack behavior: keep one stack of unmarked indices per letter; when a mirror exists, pop its top (closest), otherwise push i onto its own letter's stack.
k: One stack per letter of unmarked indices gives the closest available partner in O(1).
A consumed index is popped and never pushed again, automatically enforcing the marking rule.

a.i: For each i, walk j backward from i-1, skipping marked indices, until finding the mirror or reaching the start. O(n^2) worst case (e.g., "zzzz...a" patterns) — fine for intuition, risky at n = 1e5.
s: For each i, scan j = i-1 down to 0 for an unmarked mirror.
On success, mark both and add i - j.
a.t: O(n^2) — each index may scan back over the whole prefix.

a.i: Stacks capture 'closest unmarked' precisely: indices are pushed in increasing order, so the top of a letter's stack is its nearest unmarked occurrence. On seeing s[i], if the mirror letter's stack is non-empty, pop and score i - j; otherwise push i. Each index is pushed and popped at most once.
s: For each i: let m = mirror(s[i]); if stack[m] non-empty, ans += i - stack[m].pop(); else push i onto stack[s[i]].
a.t: O(n) — each index is pushed and popped at most once, with O(1) work per step.
a.sp: O(n) — the stacks hold at most all indices.

w: Go straight to the stack solution; the brute force is only to confirm understanding of 'closest unmarked'. Pitfalls: the mirror mapping is 25 - x (not 25 XOR tricks that fail for middle letters — actually 'a'/'z' and 'm'/'n' pairs all follow 25-x), and a matched index i must not be pushed onto its own stack. Follow-up: what if partners had to be within distance k? Then a per-letter queue/deque with expiry replaces the stack.
